The paper presents a new approach to modeling multicomponent alloy solidification using interface response functions (IRFs) for additive manufacturing.
The authors implement and compare different IRF models, including planar and dendritic growth models, and calphad coupled models.
The results show improved predictions of growth-controlled phase selection and columnar to equiaxed transition in steels and Ni-based superalloys.
The KGT model is a popular IRF model for rapid solidification, where one can obtain the interface composition and temperature as a function of solidification velocity and thermal gradient.
The Ludwig model requires fixing either solid or liquid composition at the interface, while the Wang model allows the calculation of temperature, solid, and liquid compositions at the interface.
Solute drag can consume a part of the driving force, leading to a decrease in the driving force.
The columnar to equiaxed transition (CET) is important for understanding the microstructure evolution during additive manufacturing of Ni-based superalloys.
The dendritic tip radius is related to the stability of the dendrite and can be used to predict the microstructure evolution during solidification.
The non-Fickian solute diffusion at high solidification velocities can lead to improved predictions of microstructure evolution during solidification.
At solidification velocities higher than the diffusive speed in bulk liquid, there is no solute partitioning, and complete solute trapping occurs.
The calphad coupled model for dendritic growth accounts for local non-equilibrium diffusion in liquid and can lead to improved predictions of microstructure evolution during solidification.
